desc:
Every cell of the grid holds a small integer, think of it as a letter. A cycle is a walk of length at least 4 that starts and ends at the same cell, moves up, down, left or right at each step, visits only cells with the same value as the start, and never enters a cell twice except for returning to the start at the very end. In particular, a walk may not immediately step back to the cell it just came from.

Return true if the grid contains at least one cycle, otherwise false.

grid = [[1,1,1],
        [1,2,1],
        [1,1,1]]   -> true   (the ring of eight 1s)
grid = [[1,1,2],
        [2,1,2]]   -> false
hints: Think of the cells as vertices of a graph, with an edge between two adjacent cells holding equal values. The question is whether this graph contains a cycle.
In a DFS on an undirected graph, meeting an already visited vertex that is not the vertex you just came from means a cycle exists. Pass the parent cell down the recursion (or store it on the stack).
Run the DFS from every unvisited cell, restricted to cells of the same value as the start, with an explicit stack of (cell, parent) pairs. Any visited neighbour that is not the parent proves a cycle.
editorial: Build the graph implicitly: two adjacent cells are connected when their values are equal. A connected, undirected graph is a tree exactly when it has no cycle, and a DFS finds a cycle as soon as it meets a visited vertex other than its parent. Because the grid is bipartite, any such cycle automatically has even length of at least 4, so the 'at least 4' rule in the statement needs no extra check.

Scan all cells; from each unvisited cell, run an iterative DFS that stores (cell, parent) on the stack. Mark a cell visited when it is pushed. When looking at a neighbour with the same value, skip the parent; if the neighbour is already visited, return true. If all searches finish, return false. This costs O(R · C) time and space. A union-find sweep that unites each cell with its equal up and left neighbours, and reports a cycle when they are already united, is an alternative.
